transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-06-10 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Jamie Carter (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Dr. Lena Morales (Apex), Omar Aziz (Apex), Priya Singh (Apex Sec), Ethan Park (CTO), Maya Chen (ML Lead)

[00:00] Jamie Carter: hey everyone, thanks for joining. i'm jamie from redwood, and with me is priya our solutions engineer. quick check — can everyone hear ok?
[00:05] Dr. Lena Morales: yep, loud and clear. thank you.
[00:08] Ethan Park: all good.
[00:12] Jamie: great. quick agenda — we want to understand your constraints for a private deployment, networking (vpc peering vs private endpoints), region/residency needs, and security requirements like kms and audit logs. feel free to interrupt.
[00:25] Maya Chen: thanks. i'll kick off with context — apex runs patient triage and post-op follow ups, so a lot of PHI. current infra is on aws us-east-1 and us-west-2 for some DR. we need PHI to stay in us-east-1 for primary processing due to state regs, but would like cross-region read-only replicas for analytics.
[00:45] Priya Singh: also, compliance — we need SOC2 and logs forwarded to our splunk, sso via okta, and key control via our kms/hsm.
[00:52] Priya Nair: noted. do you have an existing transit gateway or do you rely on peering today?
[00:57] Omar Aziz: we have a transit gateway connecting several accounts and partners. peering's used in a few older setups but not ideal. we're open to using private endpoints if that maps better to security.
[01:10] Jamie: OK. so with redwood private we typically offer two networking patterns: 1) VPC peering or transit-gateway style routing where the customer VPCs have direct network paths to the redwood-serving VPCs in your account/managed account; or 2) Private endpoints (aws privatelink) where traffic goes over ENIs and you don't need peering, which can simplify cross-account routing. each has tradeoffs.
[01:40] Maya: what are the latency implications for privatelink vs peering? our models are latency-sensitive for real-time triage.
[01:48] Priya Nair: good question — peering/transit-gw has slightly lower latency because it's L3 routing, but with proper ENI placement privatelink is often within a low single-digit ms difference. the bigger differences show up with egress paths and cross-az hops. we can show measured benchmarks from similar healthcare workloads.
[02:10] Dr. Lena: benchmarks would help. also curious about how you handle KV cache and model state — we have long context sessions.
[02:18] Priya Nair: our runtime manages the KV cache and we recommend colocating the serving nodes in the same AZ or region as the private endpoints to avoid inter-AZ traffic. small jitter can happen, transcription caveat: sometimes in older notes it's written as KV "cash" — ignore that.
[02:34] Ethan: (laughs) noted. on the topic of keys: can we bring our own KMS? HSM?
[02:39] Jamie: yes — we support customer-managed keys. we integrate with AWS KMS; for HSM-backed keys we'd need to discuss specifics but that's possible for enterprise plans. we also surface key usage in audit logs.
[02:52] Priya Singh: audit logs — do you emit request-level logs with PII stripped? we need to forward to our SIEM.
[02:58] Priya Nair: we can produce structured audit logs per request and you can configure retention and redaction policies. many customers forward to splunk or s3 sinks with lifecycle policies. we'll include example retention configs in the security pack.
[03:15] Maya: region constraints — we must keep PHI in us-east-1. can redwood host all control-plane components but pin compute to our VPC in us-east-1?
[03:25] Jamie: yes, typical pattern is a control plane that can be outside customer VPC, but for private deployments we can deploy serving plane into your VPCs or into a customer-managed account in the same region. the key is ensuring data plane and model compute live in the region you require.
[03:40] Omar: how about multi-region failover? if us-east-1 has an outage, can we fail over to us-west-2 without violating residency?
[03:48] Priya Nair: for PHI it's tricky. you can have a warm-standby in another region with strict controls, but live processing of PHI in another region might violate regs. some customers use async replication to west for analytics (non-PHI subset) and keep live processing in east. we'll need to define RTO/RPO and acceptable data subsets.
[04:10] Ethan: understood. let's talk ports and NAT — our security team restricts outbound egress heavily. what connectivity do you require?
[04:17] Jamie: if using privatelink, traffic goes over ENIs inside your VPC so you don't need public egress. for peering, similarly, no public internet. the control plane may need outbound HTTPS to our control plane components for metrics/heartbeats unless you opt for fully private control plane (customer-managed control plane option).
[04:40] Priya Singh: would a private control plane be an extra license?
[04:44] Jamie: yes, private control plane / on-prem options are enterprise add-ons. we can scope cost after the deep-dive.
[04:52] Maya: any constraints on IP ranges or can you work with overlapping CIDRs? we have some legacy overlapping ranges with partners.
[04:59] Priya Nair: overlapping CIDRs are painful for peering; privatelink avoids that since it's endpoint-based. if you must peer, we can use NAT or route translation but it's more operational overhead.
[05:12] Dr. Lena: network team will prefer privatelink then. what about maintenance windows and patching — we need scheduled downtimes communicated for clinical hours.
[05:21] Jamie: we offer configurable maintenance windows and SLA-backed uptimes for dedicated/reserved deployments. for private we typically align with your maintenance windows and provide advance notices and can do rolling upgrades to reduce impact.
[05:35] Omar: curious about capacity sizing — we anticipate spiky loads during morning triage. do you support autoscaling in private mode?
[05:43] Priya Nair: yes, autoscaling policies are supported. for on-prem or strict capacity you'd pick reserved capacity (dedicated) with burst options. we can recommend GPU types and concurrency targets after we see your token/sec distribution.
[05:58] Maya: can you share a sample config for autoscale thresholds?
[06:02] Jamie: we'll include example autoscale policies in the followup.
[06:06] Dr. Lena: data residency again — if we use redwood-managed model catalog, are models cached in our VPC? any model weights stored outside of our control?
[06:16] Jamie: model weights can be pulled into your private serving nodes in your VPC for private deployments so weights don't leave the region. if you require additional controls, we can discuss an air-gapped on-prem deployment.
[06:28] Priya Singh: about SSO — can you integrate with our okta instance and enforce role-based access?
[06:34] Jamie: yes, SAML/Okta SSO and RBAC are supported; we also provide audit trails per token and role.
[06:40] Omar: any network ports we need to open inbound? we are very locked down inbound.
[06:45] Priya Nair: for privatelink, you don't open public inbound ports; we create an NLB / privatelink service in our side and you create the interface endpoint in your subnets. control-plane callbacks may require outbound TLS to redwood control plane endpoints unless you choose private control plane.
[07:02] Ethan: what about data egress billing or cross-AZ costs?
[07:07] Jamie: cross-AZ transit will incur AWS charges; we recommend placing endpoints and servers in the same AZ to reduce cost. billing for compute is in your reserved/dedicated contract. network egress is billed by AWS normally. we can provide cost models comparing peering vs privatelink.
[07:22] Maya: benchmarks please — latency and cost delta.
[07:25] Jamie: yes, we'll share a benchmark spreadsheet; priya will attach measured p50/p95 latency numbers and cost-per-token approximations from similar enterprise customers.
[07:35] Priya Nair: quick note — some transcripts earlier call our private offering "redwood privatelink" or mix it up with privatelink naming; our docs clarify the naming and we'll include that doc.
[07:45] Dr. Lena: thanks. on compliance docs — can you share SOC2 report redacted and your penetration test summary?
[07:51] Jamie: yes we'll include SOC2 and pentest summaries in the security pack.
[07:56] Omar: integration-wise — how do we bootstrap keys and certs? it's important we own the KMS keys.
[08:02] Jamie: we support Bring Your Own Key for AWS KMS. for certs, mutual TLS is an option for service-to-service traffic if needed. we'll detail steps in the runbook.
[08:12] Maya: what's a typical timeline for Private deployment from kickoff to production?
[08:16] Priya Nair: depends on complexity: simple privatelink into one region can be 4-6 weeks; multi-account transit-gw + enterprise KMS + private control plane runs 8-12 weeks.
[08:29] Ethan: budgetary — rough numbers?
[08:32] Jamie: we'll share ballpark pricing: initial onboarding + monthly reserved capacity ranges. exact quotes after we get your concurrency and storage targets.
[08:41] Dr. Lena: ok. can we get an architecture diagram showing both peering and privatelink options and the control plane variants?
[08:49] Jamie: absolutely — that'll be part of the follow-up package.
[08:53] (brief cross-talk planning the SE deep-dive)
[09:05] Priya Nair: one more technical caveat — if your VPC uses strict NACLs, the interface endpoints need specific security group rules. we'll put a checklist in the doc.
[09:15] Priya Singh: perfect.
[09:18] Jamie: summary / next steps: we'll send architecture diagram, security pack (SOC2, pentest, KMS instructions), benchmark spreadsheet, and propose times for an SE-led deep dive. customer will share VPC CIDRs and a list of stakeholders.
[09:34] Ethan: sounds good.
[09:36] Dr. Lena: thanks everyone.
[09:40] Jamie: thanks all — we'll follow up by friday with the docs.

End of transcript.
